en: ☐ *Dhī*: These were merely fragments of verses found among the manuscripts in the University Library collection (numbered folios). There are three folios containing the *Catuḥstava-ṭīkā*, the *Dohākoṣa-mekhalā-ṭīkā*, and the *Adhyātmasāraśataka* composed by Nāgārjuna; these contain verses from the second half of one verse through to the final verse.

Now, this work remains incomplete without the verses (*śloka*). We have composed a commentary on it in the hope that these verses might eventually be found; however, only as far as [the verse] has been available.

It is possible that the commentary was indeed written for the entire work, as indicated by the colophon at the end: "The explanation was composed by the skillful Ācārya Paṇḍitaśiromaṇi of the Nāgara-Nepāla region."

Although the *Ṭīkā* consists solely of a partial commentary (*khaṇḍānvaya*), it has nevertheless been included here so that the labor of one scholar might not go unnoticed. The *Adhyātmasāraśataka* with Commentary, composed by Mahāpaṇḍita Śrīprabhākaragupta. Oṃ. Homage to the venerable Vajrasattva!
Since the establishment of any entity—whether earth or other elements—is nowhere possible through the various pleasures of the cessation of unity or multiplicity, nor by the many wandering Siddhas;

therefore, everything here, up to consciousness itself, is entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Because it lacks [intrinsic nature], it does not manifest spontaneously, due to the necessity of place, time, and form. || 1 ||

I shall now briefly explain, in accordance with the desire of my disciples, the commentary on the *Adhyātmasāra*, its meaning, and its collection of excellent qualities; as well as the Goddess Tārā who bestows incomparable happiness, the world which is eternally endowed with the lotus feet of the Sugata, the Dharma together with the Saṅgha, and likewise the Guru whose lotus feet are ever-present.
Just as was the desire of his kinsmen for the fame and sovereignty of his heart,
so did Śiromaṇi speak to him with words according to his ability and for their own benefit.
What does not meet and what does not dissolve?
The establishment of those [elements], earth and so forth.
How?
From somewhere, anywhere, from whatever source, or from wherever.
Who? By the perfected ones (siddhas) and their movements; by the perfected ones and their deliberations;
in what manner?
Furthermore, by what kind of many [means]?
By those consisting of the bliss of the cessation of both the one and the many.
Does it exist?
All of that.
Of what nature is it?
It ends with consciousness; furthermore, of what nature is it?
Why is there an absence of intrinsic nature?
Everywhere, on all sides.
Does not that which is manifold flash forth and manifest?
All of that, up to the limit of consciousness, [is so].
Of what? Of place, time, and form.
From what?
Why [is it] "without cause" (akasmāt)?
Because of necessity (niyamāt).
Where? In this world of saṃsāra. || 1 ||
Therefore, there exists some cause for the production of all worlds, distinct from earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness.
Whether it be this omnipresent Lord who is accepted [as such], or the Void, or otherwise; I bow to Him who is the source of all sovereignty and who is attainable through yoga. || 2 ||
Who is it that sits? Someone.
Of what nature is it?
It is the cause; of what is it the cause?
It gives birth: from what origin?
From all the worlds.
Why?
For that reason,
furthermore, of what nature is he?
Who is he who is distinct from earth, water, fire, air, ether, and consciousness?
He is the Lord.
Of what nature is he?
He is all-pervading and powerful;
furthermore, of what nature is he?
Who is the one who is beloved and esteemed?
Or of what nature is emptiness?
It is the Lord.
How?
Whether in one way or another, I bow; I pay homage.
Who? I.
Whom? [Him.]
Of what nature is that all-pervading Lord?
He is accessible through yoga, having attained meditative absorption.
What comes to be?
Sovereignty over all?
Why?
Because it is by following that [teaching]. || 2 ||
Because they do not realize this, these scholars with defiled hearts, having devised various doctrines and engaging in disputes, are mocked;
failing to attain the state of the Sugata, blinded by delusion and destroyed by death, they wander through this saṃsāra from the inauspicious to the auspicious until the end of existence. (3)
Who are these who wander and roam?
These are the wise ones.
In what? In this saṃsāra.
How?
From what [does this arise]? From the beginning of birth until the end of existence,
from the unwholesome and the wholesome.
Having done what?
Having not reached, that is, not having attained,
in this manner.
How have the learned reached the state of a sage, the path to liberation?
They were blinded by delusion and blinded by ignorance.
Furthermore, of what nature are they?
They are being mocked and ridiculed;
being of what nature [are they]?
What were they doing? Engaging in dispute and deliberation.
Having done what? Having conceptualized— that is, having applied discursive thought—
what?
Why is there a manifold view, a diverse view?
Because of lack of understanding, because of lack of familiarity.
Of what? Of that right knowledge (samyagjñāna). Of what nature is it?
Furthermore, what are those with turbid hearts and conceptual minds like?
They are ruined by death; they are seized by death. || 3 ||
In the Buddhist, Sāṃkhya, Jain, Vaiṣṇava, and Śaiva paths, the existence of rebirth is accepted through both the path of reasoning and scripture;

yet if the Cārvāka does not believe this, what can one person do for another? For the mere fact that those born blind have no experience [of light] does not mean that the moon, which truly exists, is non-existent. (4)

That which has been commenced here is the nature of things such as the composite whole (avayavin) and so forth, which is obscured from afar; how then could there be a doctrine of the sentience of the elements (bhūtacaitanyavāda) in this regard? || 5 ||
What are they that neither succeed, nor fail, nor come into existence?
They are the elements, such as earth and the rest.
Of what nature are they?
They do not succeed when non-empty, but they succeed when empty;
why is that?
By the force of valid cognition— that is, by the power of the means of knowledge— how could this not be determined?
Why is it not so?
Of what nature is that?
It is the non-establishment of the reality of the object.
Why?
Because of the departure of the one and the many; that is, because of the absence of unity and plurality.
How so?
For what reason? Because what exists?
What is this like?
It is begun and undertaken.
What?
Therein, of what nature is it? It is the essential nature of entities such as the whole (*avayavin*) and so forth.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is concealed from afar and lost from afar; by whom?
Whence [arise] the doctrine of consciousness as a material element (*bhūtacaitanyavāda*) and the doctrine of consciousness as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇacaitanyavāda*)?
Where in this world [are they found]? || 5 ||

[Objection: Even if this [collection of elements] is accepted as manifold by various schools of thought, it exists at all times within the range of everyone’s experience. Therefore, what is there to be grasped that—by virtue of being experienced—is not real even for those who accept it? For does the sky not appear here to every living being as if it were bent down? [Response: This is not so; for how could that which is not attained be considered real? (xxii) Although the collection of elements is accepted in many ways, it remains at all times within the scope of everyone’s experience. Consequently, since it is unreal even for one who accepts it based on experience, why would the sky—which appears to every person here as if it were curved—not likewise be unreal? 6.
Is there a totality?
It is the aggregate of elements, the collection beginning with earth.
Of what nature is it? Accepted where?
How is it manifold-minded?
If it exists or proceeds in any way whatsoever.
What?
A multitude of beings.
Of what nature?
That which has entered into experience— that is, that which is being perceived—
of whom? Of all beings, beginning with humans.
How so?
At all times and in every way, it is in no manner certain.
What?
Untruth, which is falsity; of what nature is it?
What is to be grasped? Of what?
Of acceptance—that is, of agreement.
Why?
Because it is that by whose experience [something is known], that is, because it is its cognition.
Why [is it not cognized]? Because of a lack of investigation.
It does not appear, it does not manifest.
What? Space.
Of what nature? Bent down, inclined.
Toward what?
"Every living being" means all sentient creatures; "where? in this cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
How?
What? || 6 ||
Furthermore, as long as the cognition of one thing does not cease until that of another arises, and as long as it does not enter the path of unconfused linguistic usage, so long is it incomplete.

Moreover, since the cessation of the cognition of one thing here occurs simultaneously with the awakening to another, if one were to accept this [as the definition of omniscience], then one who knows only a single thing would become an omniscient being who knows everything. (7)
It would not exist; it would not come to be. What?
The thought of cessation, the thought of investigation.
Of whom? Of another, of someone else.
How?
Furthermore, moreover;
where? Elsewhere.
How? Up to the point that it does not go, it does not move.
What? Something.
What?
The path of worldly activity, the course of practical conduct.
Of what nature is it?
Unmixed;
exceedingly minute.
How, then, and in what manner does it come to be?
What is that cessation? It is the state of non-existence.
Of what?
Of another?
Where? In this world of saṃsāra.
And how?
Of what [enlightenment]?
Of which other [being]?
Why? Because it exists— meaning "it is"— everywhere, on all sides.
Who? Someone.
A single knower in non-dual knowledge.
Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is the knower of all aspects (sarvākārajña), the omniscient one regarding everything.
Under what condition?
When there is acceptance of that, when there is agreement with that. || 7 ||
If the non-existence of the visible here were the sole indicator [of reality], then negation—which is never known anywhere as a relationless non-existence—would not exist;
since the establishment of difference depends on mutual reliance, all this worldly transaction is merely an illusion, just like a dream. (8)
It does not exist. What? Non-existence.
Of what nature is he?
He is absolute and non-dual.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
The non-existence of the perceptible is the non-existence of an existing entity.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is an indicator, being within the range of sensory cognition.
Where? In this saṃsāra.
How?
That which does not occur: what is it? It is the negation, the rebuttal.
Of what nature is he? He is "niḥsambandha," meaning devoid of connection.
Of what nature is he?
Known: understood.
Where? Somewhere.
Why?
Because: how indeed does it exist? What [exists]?
This is the practice, the worldly transaction;
of what nature is it?
It is all-encompassing.
Furthermore, of what nature is she?
She is characterized by delusion (*bhrānti*) and confusion (*vibhrama*).
Furthermore, of what nature is she?
It is just like a dream, resembling a dream.
Why?
For that reason.
How is it determined thus?
Why?
Because of separation—that is, because of distinction.
Of what?
Of the establishment of difference, that is, the establishment of particularity.
From what?
Because of taking refuge in mutual dependence, that is, by following upon one another's mutual reliance. || 8 ||

Just as here, even in the absence of a real entity, another birth exists—resembling an illusion or a dream—due to delusion regarding coming and going and so forth, so too, having discarded doubt arising from the words of those fallen into false views, the wise should effect the destruction of birth through the practice of yoga.
Does it exist?
Coming and going, such as departure and arrival.
Where? In this saṃsāra.
In what?
In the absence of a thing, in the absence of a substance; how? in what manner? as follows.
Why?
Because of delusion, that is, under the influence of ignorance;
it exists, it persists.
What is that?
It is the other.
What is the other?
Birth:
And how, and of what nature?
It is like an illusion and a dream; it resembles an illusion and a dream.
How?
Just so, exactly as it is.
Why?
On account of the speech of one who holds false views and has fallen [from the path], and because of following the doctrine of a nihilist;
who is to be enjoined, to be ordained, or to be made to act?
"Birth-and-death" means arising and perishing.
Having done what?
Having cast off, that is, having abandoned.
By whom? By the wise, the learned. By what?
By means of the method of practicing yoga,
what [is removed]? Doubt, that is, the state of uncertainty.
Why?
Because of the words of those fallen into false views;
and how, by whatever means possible. || 9 ||

Just as people clearly experience a distinctiveness (vaiśiṣṭya) even through falsehood, due to their connection with the diversity of the karma of the entire world, so too, through the observation of the signs of a multitude of vast virtues, a distinction will be established by the attainment of the abandonment of the fear of worldly existence, even through the practice of yoga. 10.
Who is the totality?
It is experience, the act of experiencing.
Of whom? Of people, of the world.
Of what?
Of "vaiśiṣṭya," meaning of a particularity;
like what?
Like that which.
How? Clearly.
Why?
Due to the connection with the variety of karma— that is, due to the connection with the various [results] of the auspicious and inauspicious—
by what?
By false view (mithyātva)?
Of whom?
Of all the worlds, of the entire universe.
How? In some way; it is certain that it will be accomplished—it succeeds.
What? A distinction; that is, a difference.
Of what?
Because of the accomplishment of abandoning the fear of existence— that is, because of the accomplishment described as the removal of the dread of saṃsāra—
from what [does this arise]?
From the practice of yoga, that is, from the means of yoga.
By what?
By the observation of the signs of the multitude of his vast virtues—that is, by the perception of the marks of the collection of his great qualities.
Like what?
In that same way, exactly so; somehow or other. || 10 ||
First is mastery over the body, arising from the attainment of a divine body; following that is mastery over speech, which is the power of expression resulting from the perfection of speech;
and mastery over the mind, through bringing the senses under one's own control by means of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, produced at will—thus is the supreme accomplishment. || 11 ||
Is there anything?
This is sovereignty over the body, which is freedom of the physical frame.
Why?
"First" means at the beginning.
Why?
Because of "gain," that is, because of attainment.
Of what?
Of the body; of the divine body.
It exists.
What is it?
It is the state of being a speaker, established by what has been recounted.
Of what nature is it?
But what is meant by "recounted"?
What is that? And what is that?
Mastery over speech;
of what?
Of the accomplishment of speech, that is, the accomplishment of verbal expression.
It exists.
What is it?
It is mastery over the mind and the extension of the mind.
Why?
Because of making them subject to one's own will, because of making them dependent upon oneself.
Of whom?
Of the sense faculties, such as the eye and so forth;
by what? By happiness.
It occurs.
What?
The supreme accomplishment.
By what? By the vital breaths (prāṇas) and the others; of what nature? Being produced under their own control, they are those that have arisen independently.
How?
In this manner, by this method.
How so? || 11 ||
Due to the lack of practice in yoga, one possesses a coarse view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); afflicted and subject to all manner of calamities, there is a gradual loss of vitality.
Upon the abandonment of the body, the mind—still bound by latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—comes into being once more; like a dream, it proceeds again in this very same way, and so on endlessly. (12)
It exists.
What?
The world.
Of what nature is his coarse view of a self-existent body?
Why?
Because of his lack of practice in the application of yoga.
It happens.
Who? The yogi.
Subject to every misfortune, having encountered endless suffering— of what nature is he? Afflicted, that is, possessed of disease.
It occurs.
What?
The loss of life-force.
By what?
By way of sequence; gradually.
It would be; it comes to be.
Who?
The world. Of what nature? One whose mind is bound by latent impressions (vāsanā).
Why?
Because of the abandonment of the body, that is, because of the destruction of the body.
How so?
Furthermore:
"He goes," that is, he moves.
Who? The world.
What?
That which is without beginning or end, eternal in its birth.
How?
Furthermore:
"In this way" means by this manner. || 12 ||
Because all these [channels] here are outside the flow of the circles of the vital breaths (*marut*), the extent of the limbs of the sun and moon is fifteen with a quarter;
from the transition multiplied by five and six, there is a severance of one channel with a quarter daily, following this sequence of two-fold increase. (13)
What is it that occurs?
The expansion of one's own limbs.
What is the body?
It is that of the sun and moon, i.e., the sun and the moon.
Why?
"From the flow" means from the movement;
of what? Of the mandalas, that is, the wind-mandalas.
Where?
Here, in this body.
Of what nature is the expansion of one's own limbs?
Why is he entirely outside and entirely inside? For what reason?
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
The number of Rudras is eleven; of what nature is it? It is with a quarter and with one.
It might be;
what?
That enjoyment of one's own limbs.
Of what nature is it?
It is "with a quarter," meaning accompanied by a fourth part.
Why?
From the multiplication by five, that is, from the multiplication by five of the *saṃkrāntis*;
why?
Fifty-six, that is, fifty-six plus six.
It occurs.
What is it?
It is that severance of the channels, the destruction of the *nāḍikās*.
By what? By the sequence of the number two, that is, by the order of counting as two.
How?
Daily, every day. Why? From this [point], from the solar transit (saṃkrānti). || 13 ||

In this context—the experience of one’s own self—is the intellect (dhī). Here, the seventy-two thousand channels (nāḍīs) are called "sakala" (with parts); they are seized by time due to the absence of their removal, which occurs within a hundred years.

Therefore, in the Vedas and other scriptures, that Puruṣa is described as having a lifespan of a hundred years, being differentiated by his respective months according to whether he is an Asura, a Surasura, a mortal, or others—all of them alike. (14)
It becomes what? A thousand.
Of what? Of the channels, that is, the *nāḍīs*.
To what extent?
That which is called the seventy-two [thousand channels];
where? In this body.
Of what nature is it?
It is *sakala*, meaning the collective whole (*samaṣṭi*).
Again, of what nature is it?
"Seized by time" means seized by death;
who?
That person.
Of what nature is it?
It is described, that is, uttered.
Why?
"From a hundred years" means from one hundred years.
In what? In the Vedas and so forth, that is, in the Vedas and other such scriptures.
And how? By what?
For that reason.
Why?
Because of that departure, there is no destruction of the channels. Of what nature is the person? He is one whose life-span is a hundred years, meaning his lifespan is one hundred years.
Why?
By means of their own respective internal showers.
Being of what nature?
He is distinct from asuras, suras, mortals, and so forth; that is, distinct from daityas, gods, humans, and so forth.
Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is the All. 14.

Just as the mature Sun traverses the entire zodiac, never failing to consume the moon and its lunar phases through the regular succession of its course across every sign, so too does Time revolve through this entire wheel of signs in due order; likewise, within the body, the sun and the moon [move] by means of the wheel of the vital winds (vātacakra).
It is not otherwise.
Who? The sun, the traverser.
Of what nature? Mature and capable.
To do what? To eat, to consume, to devour.
What? The constellation Ṛkṣa. Not only Ṛkṣa and the Moon;
not only the Moon and the lunar day (tithi).
Of what nature? Entire, that is, collective.
How? Thus, with certainty.
By what means? By the sequence of movement, that is, by the order of proceeding.
Why? Everywhere in the heap. Like what? Just as it revolves, that is, moves.
Who? Time, namely Rāhu.
What? This zodiacal circle. Of what nature? Entire, that is, all of it.
How? From that. By what means? By sequence, that is, in due order. In what? In the body, the physical frame.
How? For the most part, that is, generally.
How? In that very same way. And it is so.
Who? Rāhu, Time.
Of what nature? Mature and capable.
To do what? To devour, that is, to eat.
Which two? The sun and the moon.

Not only the sun and the moon, but also the wind-wheel, the collection of winds. [From the *Adhyātmasāraśataka*: Even when the body is nourished, the power within the channels, though extremely fierce in youth, reaches the top after entering the internal channel and, having taken hold of the moon, moves upward to the crown of the head.
It leads [the wind] outside the vajra and returns again to the *uṣṇīṣa*-cakra; through the destruction of the channels, one who possesses wrinkles and grey hair proceeds to the Kālacakra.
"Leads" means it causes to reach.
What? The *śakti*.
What? The moon, which is the bodhicitta.
Where? Outside, externally.
From what? From the vajra, the thunderbolt.
It approaches and arrives.
What? The crown-wheel, the wheel of stainlessness.
Having done what? Having taken up, having grasped it.

In what? On the crown of the head (*mūrdhan*). Furthermore, having done what? Having reached. What? The internal channel (*antarnāḍī*), that is, the inner tube. Being of what nature? Being "encompassed" (*parigatā*), that is, having fully pervaded it.
Where? Above, in the upper region.
Of what nature? Extremely harsh-rayed, possessing an exceedingly intense brilliance.
In what state? In youth, in the prime of life.
Under what conditions? When the body is nourished and when the moon is full. And furthermore, how does it depart? It goes forth; who? A living being.
What? The face is the wheel of time (*kālacakra*).
Being what kind [of person]? Being possessed of wrinkles and grey hair, and having shriveled skin and withered hair.
Why? Because of the destruction of the channels (*nāḍī*), that is, due to the drying up of the vessels. 16
Having abandoned even the pleasure born of passion during lunar and solar eclipses, this Caṇḍālī secretly and incessantly causes the lunar element to melt.
As long as there is decay and so forth in this world—even from childhood celibacy—therefore, embodied beings whose bodies are agitated by Śakti remain subject to time.
(17) *Drāvayet* means "she would cause to flow" or "she would cause to melt."
Who? This Caṇḍālī in the center. Whom? The lunar element.
How? Unceasingly, without interruption.
Furthermore, how? Silently, that is, without sound. Having done what? Having abandoned, that is, having avoided.
What? Pleasure.
Of what nature was it? Born of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), arising from the erotic.
How was it determined? In some way or another. Furthermore, of what nature was it? It was the time of the eclipses of the moon and the sun (*candrasūryoparāga*).
It might be;
what? Old age and so forth, such as decrepitude and the like.
Where? In this body.
How? Up to what extent? Why? Because of childhood celibacy—that is, because of celibacy from the age of sixteen downward—they somehow come to be.
Who? Embodied beings, that is, living creatures.
Of what nature are they? Subject to time, meaning under the power of death. Furthermore, of what nature are they? Their bodies agitated by [old] age, meaning their physical frames rendered infirm.
Why? Because of its state of decay.
[Verse 17] Wisdom: Generally, such a person is not seen anywhere; he exists only rarely. One should protect and maintain it.
Who? That person.
What? The pair of perishing channels, i.e., the two channels that are vanishing. From what? From yoga, that is, from meditative absorption (samādhi).
Why? Everywhere.

Why? Because of the obstruction of the path of Śaṅkhinī—that is, the blockage of the central channel (madhyamā)—by the masses of wind, which are like winds agitating the ocean of the sun and moon at the time of the eclipse (rāhu). By what means? By the collections of wind, by the multitudes of air.

Why? Because of excessive practice and excessive effort. "O Yogin! O Yogin!"—thus crying out "I, I," and filled with pride in yoga, how can this wretched man, with his hair falling out, not feel shame? For in that yoga where even results such as health are seen to be merely trivial, the delusion arises that one will attain the state of immortality through it. 19
He does not go, he does not depart;
who? the yogi;
what? shame or embarrassment.
How? By what cause? Doing what? Carrying what? What? The pride of yoga, that is, the conceit regarding yoga.
Of what nature is he? Foolish, with water-like [or dull] intellect. Again, of what nature is he? Worn out and decayed. Again, of what nature is he? With cooked hair, that is, with white hair.
What? Of what nature am I? I am a yogi.
Who? I. How? Oh, what a wonder!
It does not exist.
What? The fruit. Of what nature? Health and so forth, characterized by being free from disease and the like. Furthermore, of what nature? Not seen, not perceived.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is merely slight, that is, very small.
Where? In yoga, wherein the yogi will succeed—that is, attain it. Who? The yogi.
What? The path of immortality, the way of knowledge.
Where? In that [state]. There the yogi exists.

"What is this delusion? How has this error come about? "By some means or other. "Fie, fie upon you, fool! You who carry the pride of a yogi while your mind is agitated by passion and hatred, and who are intent on recitation like a parrot.

What is the use of those recitations that merely drain the essence from one's throat, wherein there is not even the slightest attainment of the Self? For they obstruct the merit required for the pursuit of a far greater fruit than this."
It exists.
What? Fie, fie! It is censurable.
Whom? The fool, who is devoid of knowledge.
Of what nature is it? It is "carrying. What? "Yogimāna," meaning the pride of a yogi.
From where? "Saṭitakaṭitaḥ," meaning from the loosened region of the waist.
Furthermore, of what nature is he? One whose mind is agitated by passion and hatred, whose intellect is impaired by passion and hatred.
Furthermore, of what nature is he? Devoted to recitation.
Like what? Like a parrot, like a *śuka*.
It does not exist, nor does it abide.
What? Self-acquisition, that is, the establishment of the self. By what? By those recitations.
How? What?
By what kind of things? By those that steal the nectar from the throat—that is, by those that take away the satisfaction of the throat, palate, and so forth.
Where? In which yoga.
What kind of person is it? Even one who is very small, even one who is most insignificant.
Who is he? One for whom there is an obstruction of merit consisting of the desire for greater fruits—that is, an obstruction of the merit of seeking liberation.
Why? For this reason:

20–21. Since that which was spoken by our own body [the Guru] is the entry into the reality of the inner self (adhyātmatattva) through the stabilization of knowledge and realization by means of an intellect fixed in the void;
therein, the yogi, having drunk the nectar of the inexhaustible bliss of knowledge, possesses a pure body and, therefore, being no longer fainted by any impurities, shall be liberated.
It does not exist.
Which [does not exist]? That which is yoga.
Why? Because.
Of what nature is it? It is "proclaimed by one's own body," meaning revealed through one's own physical form.
What is it?
That which is the "entry into the reality of the self" (*ātmatattvapraveśa*), that is, the manifestation of the reality inherent in the self.
By what? By the mind fixed on emptiness and the mind fixed on the path.
Why? Because of the state of being like a pillar, due to their unified nature.
Of which two? Of gnosis (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), that is, of the mind (*citta*) and its mental factors (*caitta*).
He becomes so.
Who? One whose body is translucent, being completely free from the impurities of passion and the like.
Why? Because of drinking the nectar of the imperishable bliss of perfect knowledge—that is, by drinking the immortal nectar of right cognition and inexhaustible happiness.
Where? There, in the entry into the reality of the inner self (adhyātma-tattva). What would it be? The yogi.

Of what nature is he? He is liberated, being free from all afflictions (*kleśa*). Being of what nature? He is one who has not fainted due to any impurity, being devoid of defects such as all forms of dispassion (*virāga*) and the like. Why? Because of that drinking of innate bliss (*sahajasukha*). || 21 ||

Because the paths beginning with the secret [cakra] are unassailable, we shall therefore describe the primary means for binding the wind and the mind. Having learned yoga from the feet of the Guru, through reasoning and from the scriptures, by which the knower of yoga—established in himself, possessing a steady body, and immersed in the path of non-support—becomes one whose nature is true bliss and attains the great perfection of *mudrā*.
(22) We describe; that is, we speak.
What? The preeminence of the means of integration (saṃgrahopāya), which is the primary method for binding. Of what two? Of the wind and the mind—of air and consciousness.
Why? Because of that.
Having done what? Having known and thoroughly examined.
What? Yoga. From what? From the feet of the Guru; that is, through the grace of the Guru’s feet.
Not only from the feet of the Guru, but also through reasoning;
not only through reasoning, but also from scripture, from the treatises, and from knowledge, one becomes a Perfectly Awakened One (samyaksaṃbuddha).
He goes; he proceeds.
Who? The knower of yoga. What? The accomplishment of the mudrā, which is the accomplishment of bliss. Of what nature? Great, that is, weighty.
Of what nature is he? He is one whose self is true bliss, whose self is the nature of innate bliss (*sahajasukha*).
Of what nature is he? Being immersed, being submerged—in what? In the path without support, the way of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Of what nature is he? One whose body is firm, meaning his physical form is undestroyed.
Again, of what nature is he? One who is self-abiding, being free from all afflictions and the like.
By what means? By that knowledge born of yoga. || 22 ||

First, steadiness of the breath or of the mind must be established; by means of that, a person attains the method [of yoga]. Through the pacification of even one of these two, there occurs the cessation of the other, because from both of them proceed the occurrence and the cessation of birth and death.
What is it that comes about? Steadiness—that is, stability.
Of what nature is it? It is that which is to be arranged or performed.
For whom? For Vāyu, the wind.
How so? First, at the outset—
not only of the wind, but also of the mind (cetas), that is, the consciousness (citta).
How so?
Now, "atha" is used in the sense of a doubt.
[The root] *nī* means "to lead," that is, "to cause to reach."
Who? The person, the yogi. Whom?
The means is the method.
Of what?
Of either the wind or the mind.
Where?
In that action.
By what?
By the root of the breath, that is, by the root of the prāṇa and apāna winds; what would it be? It would be so. Who? [The practitioner.]
Cessation is extinction.
Of what?
Of another mind, or of the wind.
Why?
Because of its pacification;
or because even a single transgression has been turned back through a rite of atonement.
It exists.
What is it?
It is *saṃpravṛtti*, which is to say, the process of proceeding.
It is not only the process of engagement and withdrawal that is cessation; of what?
Of birth and death—that is, of birth and dying.
By which two? By the two, namely wind and mind.
Why?
Because: || 23 ||
Among these, this one bond of breath (*vāyubandha*) grants supreme bliss to the wise: it is the restraint of the three paths within the channels (*nāḍīs*) from above and below.
When the vital air enters within these, it is the life-force of living beings; yet when it flows constantly outward, it is death and the source of all suffering. (24)
It occurs.
What is it?
This "wind-binding" (vāyubandha), which is the binding of the breath.
Of what nature is he? He is the bestower of supreme bliss, the giver of great bliss.
Of whom?
Of the wise, that is, the learned ones.
Where? In that body.
Of what nature is he?
He becomes one, without a second.
Who? [The Self.]
That which is cessation, characterized by the turning back [of the flow],
where?
Above, on high.
Not only from above, but also from below— from the lower part—
in what? In the *nālīs*, that is, in the channels (*nāḍikās*).
Of what nature are they? They are "flowing through the threefold path," meaning they proceed along the three paths. It "carries" means it brings [them] to [their destination].
Who? Death.
What?
Life means living.
Where? Outside; that is, externally.
How?
Constantly and without interruption. Of whom?
Of living beings who possess life.
How so?
Because (yat) [of] which reason (yasmāt).
Under what condition? When the Marut, the wind,
enters— that is, penetrates.
Where?
Because it is internal.
In what [things]?
Within these channels,
what is it like?
It is death, the source of all suffering.
And how? || 24 ||

He whose body is endowed with millions of postures such as the paryanka, whose skeletal frame is rigid, and who repeatedly performs the practice of carrying the pair of winds—drawing the vital breaths upward from the region of the anus by means of the uḍḍiyāna-bandha through the connection of the throat and the uvula—[attains success]. (25)
One should do; he does.
Who? The person.
What? Action, that is, performance.
How?
"Constantly" means without interruption.
Having done what?
Having joined the pair for transport—that is, having yoked them for the journey.
Of what?
Of the wind. Being in what state?
His body is joined with the paryanka posture; his body is endowed with the paryanka seat. Furthermore, of what nature is he? He has a rigid backbone, meaning his spinal column has been made firm.
Having done what?
Having contracted.
How?
"Highly" means to an extreme degree.
Why?
Because it originates from the "seat of the anus," that is, from the location of the anal passage.
Why?
From bondage. Of what?
Of Uḍḍiyāna, which is the Atala-cakra.
And how? Not merely by contracting, drawing up, and bringing [them]—those vital breaths (asūn), that is, the prāṇa-winds.
Where?
Above, above that which has fallen away.
From what?
From the throat, by means of the application of the mechanism of the *ghaṇṭikā*, from the location of the cavity at the back of the palate. || 25 ||
When the fire, resembling lightning, comes under one's control because the wind has been brought into subjection by forceful drawing into one’s own heart;

then, with the moon-like [breaths] that grant pure bliss, which have issued from the uvula (*lambikā*), one should incessantly satisfy the mass of the drying channels (*nālī*) with those very foods. || 26 ||
It prevails; it comes into being.
What? Fire, the flame.
Of what nature?
Resplendent like lightning, resplendent like a thunderbolt.
When?
When— at which time?— at what being present?
At [the teacher] having been brought near, at [him] being present.
In which wind? In the wind of wisdom (dhī-vāyu).
Where?
In one's own heart, in the lotus of the heart.
How?
Self-dependence means being dependent on oneself.
By what?
By means of attraction;
of what kind?
By the strong, the most powerful.
How?
In this manner, by this method;
he should satisfy—that is, he thoroughly satisfies.
Who? The person (puruṣa).
What?
A mass of drying stalks— that is, a collection of withering tubular vessels— by what means?
By the moon-like shells (or, by the moistened [śuklaiḥ] ones).
Of what nature were they?
They were produced and abundant. From where?
From the *lambikā*, from the location of the wheel of purity (*vaimalyacakra*).
Furthermore, by what kind of moons?
By those that bestow stainless bliss, that is, those that bestow innate bliss (*sahajasukha*).
How?
In this manner, by this method. Why?
From this means of accomplishment;
not only by means of the moon and the foods.
How so?
"Thus" means in that manner. How so?
"For that reason. || 26 ||

Sometimes there may also be a deficiency of digestive fire (*vahni-māndya*) due to [excessive] drinking, food, and so forth; this is called the "secret of secrets. One should strike and draw up that which is the triangular element of fire (*agni-bhūta*) by means of the wind (*pavana*), whereby, having become ignited at the navel and pervading the entire body, it spreads bliss. (27)
It would be; it becomes.
What?
A deficiency of fire, that is, a paucity of digestive heat.
By what? By means of drinks, food, and so forth—namely, substances for drinking, food, and the like.
In some way or another.
Furthermore, how?
At some time, on a certain occasion.
Having done what?
Having struck and suppressed—
what? That which.
Of what nature is it? It has become fire. Again, of what nature is it?
A triangle.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is "stated," meaning described.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is more secret than the secret, more profound than the profound.
"In this manner" means by this method.
And how should one cause it to blaze, cause it to flare up? Who? The yogin.
What is that?
Is it become fire?
Having done what?
Having drawn in and brought forth.
And how? From where? From the wind, that is, from the air.
And how? Where?
At the navel, within the calyx of the navel-lotus.
By what cause?
It extends and increases.
What [does so]?
Fire;
what? Bliss, that is, the state of happiness.
Having done what? Having become, that is, having come into being.
Of what nature was he?
"Blazing" means ignited.
Having done what? Having pervaded, that is, having completely filled.
Why? Because it exists in the entirety of the body, that is, in the whole physical frame. || 27 ||

Since the Vajra-issuing power (*vajrāntī śakti*) blazes from this secret lotus of thirty-two petals into the navel-lotus consisting of sixty-four petals, [it proceeds] into the heart-lotus endowed with eight stainless petals, from the throat into the tooth-petal [lotus], into the half of the secret lotus, and into the four-petaled Brahma-aperture at the head. (28)
The *Adhyātmasāraśataka* blazes and shines forth. What is it? It is power—the power of vital breath (*prāṇa*).
In what?
In the navel, in the *nirmāṇa*-lotus.
Of what nature is it?
In a lotus consisting of sixty-four petals;
and how, being of what nature?
While moving, that is, while going.
Why?
Because [it arises] from the secret lotus, from the wheel of fire.
Of what nature is it?
It has thirty-two petals.
Where?
In this body— not only in the lotus of the heart, which consists of sixty-four petals— but also in the heart-lotus. In what state?
In that which possesses eighteen petals— not only in the heart-lotus, but also in the throat and the throat-petals—
of what nature?
On the tooth-leaf with thirty-two petals;
not only on the throat, but also on the head, in the head-lotus.
Of what nature is it?
For the sake of the secret lotus, that is, within half of the secret lotus;
not only on the head, but also in the Brahma-aperture, which is the wheel of stainlessness (*vaimalyacakra*).
In what state is it?
On the four-petaled [lotus].
And how? 28.

Just as these wheels—earth, water, fire, air, ether, and consciousness—burn all the sense organs and so forth when thus purified, so too does the moon [the vital breath] flow from me once I am burnt; for the power, impelled with force through the central channel, enters everywhere pervading the tube.
It burns the six wheels, which are lotuses. Of what nature are they?
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, and consciousness are pure—meaning the earth, water, fire, wind, space, and mind are purified—in this manner, by this method.
How?
In this way.
And it burns. What?
Power.
Which ones?
The sense organs: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Of what nature are they?
"Nikhilāni" means all or entire. What is it that flows and moves? Who?
The moon is the bearer of the hare (śaśabhṛt).
Under what condition?
When ignorance has been consumed and wisdom is blazing.
Like what?
Like that; in that manner.
Having done what?
Having pervaded and completely filled— what? The channel (nāḍī), that is, the small tube (nāḍikā).
Why? From everywhere and in every place;
it enters and it penetrates.
What is the power?
In what [does it reside]?
In the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*);
being what state?
Being set in motion and being cherished.
Why?
Because [it arises] from the wheel.
From what?
By force, with effort. || 29 ||

Through gnosis, through emanation, and likewise here through the enjoyment of the Dharma, these glorious blisses are proclaimed to arise sequentially from the purification of the body by means of consciousness; they indeed cause the growth of the entire physical form, and then, having filled the six glorious wheels which bestow all happiness, one proceeds like the moon.
"Should go" means "should proceed.
Who? The moon, Indu.
Having done what? Having filled, that is, having completely filled.
What things?
The six glorious wheels (śrī-ṣaṭ-cakrāṇi).
Of what nature are they? They are bestowers of all happiness, that is, givers of every kind of bliss.
Furthermore, of what nature are they?
They are called "thī," meaning they have been illustrated.
Which ones?
Furthermore, what are these like? They are the nourishers of the entire body, that is, those which cause the whole body to grow.
How?
Just so.
And how?
How?
Immediately thereafter.
By what?
By purity of body, that is, by the purity of the Tathāgata’s body. Why? Because of knowledge.
Not only from knowledge, but also from emanation;
where?
Here, in this body.
Not only by way of emanation, but also by way of the enjoyment of the Dharma.
How?
In that manner, in that way.
Not only through the enjoyment of the Dharma, but how also through glorious happiness? Gradually, step by step.
Where? Here, in this body; not only from glorious happiness, but also from higher knowledge. || 30 ||
Having completed seventy-two thousand channels (nāḍikās), that moon proceeds to the full vajra;

through its continuity, it goes upward again by means of drawing [the breath] in the same way, and thus one's own body is perfected repeatedly through the method of inhalation into the upper wheel. // 31 //
Who goes? Who moves? The moon.
Whom? The thunderbolt, the diamond.
Having done what? Having done what? A thousand, that is, ten hundred; of what? Of the *nāḍikās*, that is, the tubes (*nālīs*).
Of what nature is it? It is called the seventy-two-fold.
Of what nature is it? It is complete, perfectly full, in every way.
Again, why? Because of continuity—that is, because of connection—of what? Of these seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍī*).
How? Up to...
Who goes? Who moves? That power. What is it? The upper wheel, the uṣṇīṣa wheel.
By what? By the drawing; by what was it drawn? Excessively;
how? Furthermore.
How? In that manner, in that way, it is perfected; what is perfected? The body.
By the method of breath-control, through the practice of being without breath;
how? Again and again, repeatedly. || 31 ||

When the moon and the sun, having moved from their respective positions in the upper and lower [channels], become equalized within the central channel and pervade the entire body by being released from their bonds— for that reason,
he creates or fashions.
What is this? It is the "Wheel of Channels" (nāḍikācakra), that is, the system of channels (nāḍīcakra).
What [is it]? It is the *Adhyātmasāraśataka*. What is the body (deha)? It is the physical frame (śarīra). Of what nature is it? It is new (nava), meaning fresh.
How is it thus uncertain? And again, by what means? By the attainment of life—that is, by the attainment of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*).
How so? Exceedingly—by what [means]? Thereafter follows the state of the equal flavor (*samarasa*) of the moon and the sun.
Of what nature is it? Even though dead, even though it has gone to death—of what nature is this wheel of channels (nāḍikācakra)? It is situated within the wheel. || 32 ||

One who is devoted to the practice of this yoga, being free from poison at first, abandons all diseases of the body; even at seventy years of age, with full cheeks and lips, he becomes as if possessed of a youthful frame, with black hair, for half a year—provided he practices constantly, eats moderately, and remains celibate. || 33 ||
Who is he? That yogi;
of what nature is he? Free from poison, free from sense objects.
Where? At the beginning, first of all;
being what kind of person? Being one who practices [his] duties constantly;
and again, being what kind of person? One devoted to the practice of yoga, that is, one intent upon the practice of yoga.

Of what nature was he? One whose cheeks and lower lip were full—that is, one whose cheeks and lower lip were like the full moon. Having done what? Having abandoned—that is, having cast aside—what? A body entirely afflicted with disease—a body covered by many illnesses.
How, then, is he? Of what nature is this yogi who has reached seventy years—seventy years of age?
Of what nature does he become? One with a fresh body—a new physical form.
Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is one who eats moderately, eating with restraint.
Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is a celibate (*brahmacārī*), delighting in the imperishable bliss of union with the Mudrā. || 33 ||

If, after six months, having perceived himself to be composed of passion alone, he were to test his entire stability here by sporting with a hundred women and experiencing the intense bliss born of sexual union, yet the moon did not depart from his body, then he would have attained a perfected form.
Who is he? A yogi.
Of what nature is he? One whose body is perfected, meaning one whose physical form is not destroyed.
When? At that time; who would not go, would not proceed?
The moon, the lord of the night.
What? Outside. How?
Having done what? Having eaten, that is, having consumed.
What? The bliss born of sexual union, the pleasure of passion with a beloved woman. How? Intensely, that is, continuously.
Where? In that [spiritual] practice.
Having done what? Having performed what? [He performed] the act of play, such as laughter, dancing, and so forth; with whom? Together with [them].
By what? Even by a hundred women, or even by a hundred thousand lovely women—what could be done? To weigh, that is, to measure it; what? Stability, which is steadfastness.
Of whom? Of that moon.
What [is it]? Here, in this body.
Having done what? Having beheld, having gazed upon.
Whom? Oneself. Of what nature? Consisting of passion (*madana*). Again, of what nature? Consisting of joy (*nanda*). Furthermore, of what nature? Entirely (*sarva*), that is, completely.
How [is it] "beyond six months," that is, above six months? || 34 ||

Taking the worldly happiness of those of virtuous fame as a point of reference, the yogi beholds his own incomparable bliss in the form of primordial wisdom; possessing inexhaustible glory, freed from the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable, omniscient and with a translucent body, he wanders at will out of compassion to protect the multitude of afflicted beings. (35)
Who wanders and roams? The yogi.
By what means? By his own will, according to his own desire.
To do what? To protect and to deliver.
Whom? The multitude of people, the mass of beings. By what means? By compassion, by pity.
Of what nature is it? It is afflicted (*ārta*), tormented by the sufferings of old age, death, and so forth.
Having done what? Having observed (*samīkṣya*)—that is, having looked at—what? One's own self (*svam ātmānam*).

Of what nature is it? It is incomparable bliss, meaning bliss that transcends all comparison, which is to say innate bliss (*sahajasukha*). Furthermore, of what nature is it? It has the form of gnosis, meaning its essential nature is gnosis (*jñāna*).
Of what nature is that yoga? It is "puṇyaśloka," consisting of merit.
Having done what? Having made it the object of focus, having fully relied upon it.
What [is that]? The pleasure of sense objects, the pleasure derived from the enjoyment of the five desires.
Furthermore, of what nature is he? He possesses inexhaustible glory (*akṣayaśrī*), meaning his splendor is undiminished.

Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is free from the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable (*kleśajñeyāvṛtivirahita*), meaning he is devoid of the veil of afflictions and the veil of the knowable. Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is all-knowing (*sarvavit*), an omniscient one (*sarvajña*), who understands the occurrences of the three times within the world situated in the three realms of consciousness (*jñānadhātutraya*).
Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is one whose body is transparent, a body that has transcended all conceptual constructions. || 35 ||
Therefore, Ānanda, these four initiations which have been described here are not to be accomplished through the pleasure of the organs; rather, they are merely illustrative examples.

Consequently, the goal is immovable bliss, and this is the path for the attainment of all virtues, consisting of the means [of practice] through the binding of the moon and the syllable (akṣara). || 36 ||
Who are they? These [blisses]—the first bliss and so forth—are what blisses? Those which...
Of what nature are they? They are described, that is, proclaimed;
where? Here, in this practice.
Of what nature are they? Fourfold, meaning of four kinds.
Why? From the consecration (*sekataḥ*), that is, from the empowerment (*abhiṣekāt*), which ones do not arise? They are the joys (*ānandāḥ*).
Of what nature are they? They are to be accomplished, meaning they are to be brought about through the pleasure of the instruments—that is, from the pleasure of the senses.
How so? Indeed.
Furthermore, of what nature are they? They are merely illustrations; they are merely examples. (From the *Adhyātmasāraśataka*, verse 10).
What? The means of proof (sādhana). Of what nature? That which is to be proven (sādhya), that which is to be established.
Why? For that reason.
Of what nature is the means? It is unswerving bliss, which is to say, uninterrupted bliss.
Who is it that becomes so? The syllable-moon, the imperishable moon.
Of what nature is the goal to be accomplished? Why? From bondage—that is, from being bound—of what? Of the wind, the air;
and in what manner?
Who is "there"? What is the path? This very one is it.
For what? For the attainment of all virtues, for the abundance of every excellence. || 36 ||

From wind [the body] becomes like that; and thus, through the practice of ritual action by a complete ascetic, the accomplishment of the body arises from mercury. That bound metal, possessing blazing majesty and abandoned faults such as passion, must also be sought by us from the *Drumatilaka* treatise. || 37 ||
What comes into being, what arises? Accomplishment, that is, perfection; of what? Of the body, of the physical form.
Why? From wind—that is, from the air;
what is it like? It becomes just like that.
What? A metal such as copper. Of what nature? Bound and perfected.
From what? From *sūta*, that is, mercury (*pārada*).
How? In this manner. And how does it come to be?
Who? That essence—the essence of air—is of what nature? It is to be served, that is, worthy of being cultivated.
By whom? By the "akhilayati," that is, by the complete yogi. From what? From the practice of karma—that is, from the practice of the *kunduru* rite—it comes to pass.
Who? The element—the lunar element.
Of what nature is it? One whose greatness is blazing, having kindled its majesty. Being of what nature? Bound—that is, firmly fixed.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is one whose defects such as attachment (rāga) have been abandoned, just as the defect of being reddened by copper and the like is abandoned.
What is it that becomes so? That essence (rasa), namely the essence of air (vāyu-rasa).
Of what nature is it? It is to be sought after, that is, to be followed.
From where? From the text (*grantha*).
From which text? From the *Drumatilaka*, that is, from the one named *Drumatilaka*.
Of whom? Of us; in some way or other. || 37 ||

Or rather, having abandoned all ritual actions and the like, one should practice vajra-recitation, which is the means for attaining bliss and the cause for stabilizing the wind and space, by clearly following the true mantra through the realization of the meaning of the three syllables, due to the discernment of the circles of wind located in both nostrils. (38)
Who should practice? Who should engage in activity? The yogi; what? Vajra-recitation.
Having done what? Having abandoned or relinquished what? External actions such as ritual acts; in what state are they? Entirely, that is, completely.
How? Or what is this vajra-recitation like? It is the means for bliss, the method for attaining innate bliss (*sahajasaukhya*).
Furthermore, how is it characterized? It is the cause for the stability of wind and space, the cause for the stabilization of air and ether.
Why? Because it is present everywhere; from what? Because of its following, that is, its attainment;
of what? Of the true mantra.

Of what kind [of word]? Of that which consists of three syllables, such as the *oṃkāra* and others. By what means? By the comprehension of meaning (*arthagatyā*), that is, by the understanding of the sense.
How? Clearly (*sphuṭaṃ*), that is, manifestly (*vyaktam*).
Why? Because of discernment—that is, from investigation—of what?
Of the circles of wind located in the two nostrils; that is, of the five circles beginning with wind that have reached the two nasal passages. || 38 ||

Because the wind blows within this emanation-lotus consisting of sixty-four petals, it emerges through the paths of the moon and the sun into the nostrils in five ways as mandalas— yellow, white, red, green, and dark— corresponding respectively to earth, water, fire, air, and space.
It blows, it moves;
what? The wind.
In what?
In this "emanation-lotus," the lotus of the navel.
Of what nature is it?
It consists of sixty-four petals.
Why?
Because of the taking up and casting aside [of the breath].
By what?
By the path of the moon and sun, that is, by the route of the sun and the moon.
Why?
From the emergence, that is, from the arising;
in what? In the nostril, the cavity of the nose.
By what? By the mandala.
In five ways, that is, in five modes.
Why?
From the hips, water, fire, wind, and space—from earth, water, fire, air, and ether.
By what? [By the mantra.]
In the sequence of yellow, white, reddish-brown, green, and dark-blue colors. || 39 ||
Having touched the base, the earth flows below; on the left side flows water, fire on the right, wind above, and space enters the center.
Beginning from twelve finger-breadths here, it then proceeds in sequence up to sixteen, increasing outward until it again enters the secret lotus.
It carries; it moves.
What?
The earth, the ground.
Having done what?
Having touched, that is, having made contact with.
What?
"Below" means the lower part. And what does it carry?
"Toya" means water.
Where? On the left side, that is, the left portion.
And it carries.
What? Fire.
Having done what?
Having touched.
What?
The left [hand] carries the right side.
Who?
The wind is the air;
where? Above.
For how so?
And it carries.
What?
The sky is the atmosphere. Having done what would it be touched?
What?
The middle region, that is, the central part.
Having done what?
Having begun from [there].
What?
The *Adhyātmasāraśataka*, twelve finger-breadths [in length].
Twelve finger-breadths.
Where?
Here, in this body, the physical frame.
Of what nature is it?
It ends at the sixteenth [digit]. Why? Because of the sequence following from that.
In what? Outside, externally.
By what?
By one who has grown with growth.
He enters.
How?
Furthermore:
what?
The secret lotus, the wheel of the palm.
How?
Until what limit?
And how? || 40 ||
In this context, by means of withdrawal (saṃhāra), the earth [element] is first in the right nostril; by means of emanation (sṛṣṭi), space is in the left;

and by the transition between both flows, there is the movement of fifty-six breaths of the time-artery (kālanāḍī). This transition occurs with eighteen hundred and twenty-five breaths over a period of five dandas.
It exists.
What is it?
It is the earth, the ground.
In what? In the nostril; specifically, the right one.
How?
Formerly, in the past; where?
Here, at the transition.
By what?
By the withdrawal, that is, by dissolution.
It comes to pass.
In what?
In the left nostril.
By what? By the creation, that is, by the process of emanation.
It exists.
What?
The sky, the ether?
What is the body?
It is the vehicle; it exists on both the left and the right.
What?
The vehicle of the wind, that is, movement by means of the air.
How many?
Fifty-six.
Of what kind? Accompanied by a quarter—that is, joined with a fourth part.
Of what?
Of what [does it consist]? Of the central channel (madhyamā), the time-vein (kālanāḍī).
What comes into being? [It] comes into being.
Who? [The subject].
"Transition" means the act of passing over. By what means? By five staffs.
By what? By breaths. Of what kind?
By those who have reached one hundred and eight [years]. || 41 ||
And thus, through twelve transitions on both sides, the vital breath (prāṇa) moves for sixty daṇḍas, along with two thousand six hundred and ten [breaths].

As for the four times of enjoyment (kālabhoga) mentioned here regarding the two junctional channels (sandhyānāḍī), they are not spoken of as [separate] exhalations, because they are extremely difficult to perceive in the path of worldly convention.
[The word] "yāti" means "goes."
What?
The vital breath, the prāṇa-vāyu. By what means?
By sixty *daṇḍas*; by what?
By the *saṃkramas*, that is, the solar transits (*saṃkrāntis*).
By how many? By twelve. Why?
"Abhitaḥ" means on all sides.
How?
"Ittham," meaning in this manner.
And how? Furthermore, by what kind [of beings]?
By hundreds of directions—that is, by thousands (ten hundreds).
By what kind? By more than what? By six hundred.
How?
Two joined with two non-units [make] four.
They exist.
"Spoken" means uttered. Which ones?
The junction-nāḍīs (sandhyānāḍyaḥ). Of what nature are they?
The lords of the periods are eclipsed by Rāhu.
How and where?
In this body.
How? Because (yat), for which reason.
How many?
Four; they have four measurements.
Furthermore, what are these channels like?
They are not liberated, nor have they been liberated.
They have been described as such.
Wherein?
On the path of worldly transaction, on the way of conventional usage.
Why?
Because it is exceedingly difficult to discern, that is, because it is impossible to perceive.
Of what? Of those channels (nāḍīs). || 42 ||
Alternatively, having made fifty-six *jala-palas* plus one-quarter, sixty-four *daṇḍas* should be established here for a day and night.

Since this *jala-pala* consists of six breaths, and there are sixty of them in a *daṇḍa*, one should set aside that [measure] and employ the flow of breath (*vāyuvāha*) for the sake of practical usage. (43)
What are they? They are the sixty-four staffs (daṇḍas).
Of what nature are they?
They are to be performed; by whom?
By means of punishment;
what [is it]?
Day and night, throughout the day and night.
Where?
Here, in this treatise on luminaries (jyotiḥśāstra).
Having done what?
Having prepared and refined what? A *pala* of water, that is, a *pala* of liquid.
How many? Fifty-six.
Of what nature?
Or with a quarter [of a mora].
And how?
How?
And then, immediately after that, what happens? What [is it]?
"Vāyuvāha" means one who carries the wind. Of what nature is he? He is "niyojya," meaning he is to be employed.
In what?
In the performance of worldly transactions (vyavahṛtikṛte), that is, in the carrying out of legal or conventional dealings.
Having done what?
Having abandoned, having relinquished;
what?
That punishment.
It occurs. What is this "pala of water"? By whom?
By breaths;
by how many? By six.
It exists.
What?
The staff.
By how many?
By sixty *pānīya-palas*.
Where?
Wherein || 43 ||
By the wind, this entire mechanical body of embodied beings is thus opened up; through the application of karma, it assumes various forms that bestow both pleasure and pain.
As long as the vital breath dwells within this body, it lives; by its departure, death comes. Apart from this wind, there is no other agent within the body. (44)
He worships and performs [action].
What?
The machine of the body. What? [The act of worship.]
It has various forms and various manifestations.
Of what nature is it?
It is the giver of happiness.
It is not only a giver of happiness, but also a giver of suffering.
Why?
Because of the conjunction of karma—that is, through the meeting of auspicious and inauspicious actions.
Furthermore, in what manner is this bodily machine?
It is both expanded and contracted.
By what means?
By the wind, that is, by the air. Of what nature? Entire, meaning complete.
How?
In this manner; thus, he lives.
Who?
An embodied being, a living creature.
Under what condition?
While he dwells— that is, while he makes his abode—
in what?
In this vital breath (prāṇavāta).
In what?
In the body, in the physical form; what comes? What arrives?
Death.
Why? Because of departure.
The meaning is "due to the exit of the wind from the body. What is it that does not exist?
The author is the creator of the *Adhyātmasāraśataka*.
Who?
Another, i.e., someone else.
Where? From the body, that is, from the physical frame.
Having done what?
Having abandoned what? The wind, that is, the vital breath (prāṇa-vāyu).
Why?
For that reason. || 44 ||
That which, having entered [the body], removes the entire web of defects from the physical frame; which, upon reaching death, bestows a state of immortality corresponding to its own nature;
and which, having attained bondage for a very long time, grants the bliss of liberation—such is the one Lord Vāyu, who exists both within the worldly realm and beyond it. (45)
It carries away; it withdraws.
What? That which is the wind.
What? The web of defects, that is, the collection of defects such as disease and so forth. Why?
From the body, that is, from the physical frame;
having done what?
Having fainted, that is, having fallen into a swoon.
It restrains and gives;
who? Vāyu.
What?
The state of immortality.
Of what nature?
One who is suitable to oneself;
that is, one who resembles oneself.
But how, indeed, by doing what?
Having gone where?
To death— that is, to dying.
It exists.
What? Wind.
Of what nature is he?
He is the bestower of the bliss of liberation (mokṣa-saukhyapradātā), the giver of the happiness of emancipation.
Why?
"Abhitaḥ" means on all sides.
How?
"Suciram," for a very long time.
Having done what?
Having obtained— that is, having attained—
whom?
Bondage means being bound.
Who is it?
Vāyu; of what nature? The Lord (īśa), the Sovereign (īśvara).
Of what nature is he? He is one, without a second. Why?
"By virtue of having a supramundane object" means by virtue of having an object that transcends the world.
In what?
In the world—that is, in the three worlds.
Of what nature?
Entire, that is, complete. || 45 ||

Having abandoned this body, the wind—divided fivefold as prāṇa, apāna, and then samāna, udāna as the fourth, and vyāna as the fifth—carries the breath everywhere and experiences enjoyments; yet, through the recitation of the Vajra-syllable, it rendered the three kinds of bliss-akṣaras incomparable.
He compares; he follows.
Who? The yogin.
Or what?
Three syllables.
How many?
In three ways.
Having done what?
Having understood, that is, having known.
What?
It becomes one that has the wind as its vehicle, i.e., one carried by the wind.
What?
All accomplishments.
Why?
From the recitation of the three-syllable Vajravarṇa, it comes to pass.
Who? This wind.
Of what nature is it?
"Fivefold" means of five kinds;
in what?
In the body, that is, the physical form.
Of what nature is it?
It exists and is possessed of differentiation.
And how so?
Having done what?
Having abandoned.
How so?
How? Five.
Which?
The out-breath; not only the out-breath, but also the in-breath.
How so?
Thereafter, subsequently. And how?
It comes to be.
Who?
Even the Samāna;
not only the Samāna, but also the Udāna.
Of what nature is it?
It is the fourth; not only udāna and vyāna.
And likewise: Intellect resides in the heart; prāṇa in the anus; samāna in the region of the navel;
udāna should be in the region of the throat; and vyāna pervades the entire body. (46)

Having offered this into the fire of the mantra, we shall now understand, in accordance with the reality of the Great Sacrifice (*mahāyāga*), those who possess various powers and abide within it; furthermore, what is the doorless state, what is the constant attachment, what is the bond, what is above, what is the command of the Guru, what is derived from the scriptures, what is the composed state, and what are the enjoyments at hand? (47)
Why [is it] given to the mantra? Because, according to the principle of the Great Sacrifice (*mahāyāga*), we [are] the self of many fourfold great mantras within the fire.
Of what nature are they?
They possess various strengths (*vividhabalinaḥ*), meaning they have many kinds of markings (*likhyāḥ*).
Of what nature are they?
"Abhyantarasthāḥ" means situated within;
of what? Of that mantra.
And how [is it] heavy?
And how [is it] entirely from all doors, entirely...? How? Subsequently, afterwards.
And how does it come to be?
Who?
Bondage: the bondage of pleasure.
Of what nature [are they]?
Immovable. Not only—how is the scriptural statement?
It is relevant and abundant.
And how [is it so]? Because of enjoyments. (47)

First, one should provide the primordial vowel (A), and likewise that [vowel] ending in the sixteenth (Ū) in the middle; at the end, one should give the remaining consonant together with the supreme (M). Again, at the beginning and the end, there is a vowel, and furthermore the fifth [consonant] ending in the fifth (Ņ); then the crescent moon (Bindu) and the void (Visarga), joined with the qualities and conjoined with the name of the one to be accomplished (Sādhya). || 48 ||
Who bestows, and to whom does the yogi give?
What is that which, by means of attainment, places the first vowel, the letter *a*, at the very beginning?
What is the yogin?
The vowel ending in the fifth [consonant], which is the syllable *u*.
Of what nature is that which ends at the sixteenth?
In what [does it reside]?
How, then, in the middle?
How?
In that manner, in that way, as before;
how so?
Immediately thereafter, he should bestow [it].
Who? The yogi. What?
What?
The consonant *ha* followed by another [consonant]— of what nature is it? It is stainless (*amala*), being devoid of its own vowel (*svara*).
In what?
At the end, in the remainder,
one should bestow it.
Who? The yogi.
Whom? [Himself.]
To which [deity] should one first bestow the fifth vowel, the syllable *u*, at the very beginning?
Who? The yogi. Which sound?
* [In the manuscript of this verse, only the latter half of the second quarter and the first half of the third quarter were found;
as for the commentary, the scholar Paṇḍita relied solely on that fragmentary commentary, and I have attempted, with some difficulty, to complete the words.
One's own reading is indicated within brackets [ ]. The *Adhyātmasāraśataka* ends with the fifth vowel, the letter *ū*;
in what?
At the end, that is, at the conclusion.
How so?
Who, moreover, should bestow it again and again?
The yogi [perceives] the "fragmented moon" as the half-moon,
while "space" (kha) is emptiness.

Why? Because of the conjunction with qualities; that is, due to the conjunction with qualities such as the syllable *oṃ*. Of what nature is it? It is "joined with the goal," meaning accompanied by that which is to be accomplished.
How so? Immediately thereafter. || 48 ||

By virtue of internal absorption, the syllable OṂ is the Moon, the cause of emanation; therein, the syllable ĀḤ is the Sun, transformed by power and the establisher; the syllable HŪṂ, by way of bringing about the destruction of impurities, is Rāhu, the bringer of the end; therefore, the attainment of the equal flavor of these [syllables] must be accomplished through vajra-recitation. || 49 ||
Who is he? The syllable Om.
Of what nature is he? Why is he called the Moon?
On account of the internal movement of the hundredfold mind,
how is he characterized? He is the cause of creation, the cause of origination.
Where? It exists there, in the body.
Who?
That form; of what nature is it?
Furthermore, of what nature is Bhānu Āditya?
He is the establisher, the one who brings about stability.
Of what nature is it?
It is "transformed involuntarily," because it arises from an independent transformation.
What? The syllable *hūṃ*. Of what nature is it?
Furthermore, what is Rāhu like?
He is the bringer of the end, the agent of dissolution.
Why?
Because it causes the destruction of merit (*asukṣaya*), that is, because it causes the destruction of living beings (*prāṇakṣaya*).
It comes into being [in this way].
What is it?
It is the state of equal flavor; how is that state? It is a state of equality.
To whom should she be made subject?
To these [planets], beginning with the Moon.
Why? Because of vajra-recitation;
why?
For that reason. || 49 ||

One should observe with an unswerving mind the vital air (*prāṇavāta*) as it issues forth, follows the *praṇava*, and remains within, throughout all states, until the *nālī*—the duration of sixteen hundred and twenty breaths—is completed; through this, the mind enters the inconceivable reality. || 50 ||
Who should observe and contemplate? The yogi;
whom? [The breath.]
The vital air, the breath— of what nature?
It is departing, going out.
What? The syllable *hūṃ*.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
What is situated?
The vowel *ā*, namely the phoneme *ā*.
Where?
Within;
in what manner is the yogi?
With unshakable intellect and steady intellect—
in what?—
in all states, that is, in the conditions of body, speech, and mind.
How so?
Who is it that exists?
Entry into the inconceivable reality; entry into the innate reality belongs to what?
To the mind.
Why?
Because of the breaths of the *nālī*; that is, from the breaths of the *nāḍikā*.
Of whom?
Of how many hundred [breaths] is it? Of twenty thousand breath-winds, that is, of two myriads of winds; of what kind? Of several hundreds.
How [is it] for the sixteen?
One who is skilled in his own welfare should contemplate this beautiful form—the secret of secrets—either in brief or according to one's own preference as a mantra-convention:
the syllable *oṃ*, through which the breath enters as the seed of all prosperity, and the syllable *hūṃ*, through which it skillfully ascends by means of the yoga of the uvula. || 51 ||
Who should contemplate?
The yogi.
What is this? It is the convention of mantras, the secret of mantras; of what nature is it?
Furthermore, how is that which is concise and brief characterized?
It is the secret of secrets, the profound of the profound.
Why?
By the power of its own nature, that is, by the power of its self-designation;
how so?
Or, in case of doubt:
what kind of yogi?
One who is skillful in his own welfare, that is, one who is discerning regarding his own benefit.
Of what nature is the secret convention of mantra?
It is of beautiful form and pleasing luster; furthermore, of what nature is it?
Entering— making an entry—
into what? Into the wind (anila).
By what? By the syllable Om. Furthermore, of what nature is it?
Furthermore, what is the seed of all prosperity and the cause of all success like? It is "skilled in ascending," meaning expert in moving upwards.
By what? By the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
How?
Preceded by the union with the uvula, it is the first meeting with the uvula. || 51 ||

For the yogi whose mind is thus engaged in the practice of breath-control (vāta), neither the act of begging for alms nor excessive eating is appropriate; likewise, sleep, the muttering of prayers, the forceful suppression of breath through *haṭha*, recitation, worship, fire-offerings (*homa*), and so forth must also be abandoned during this state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). || 52 ||
What does not exist, does not come into being?
Food.
Of what nature is it?
Furthermore, of what nature is that which is even more abundant?
How could it not be logical and appropriate?
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is the act of begging for alms.
And how, and of whom?
Of what kind of yogi?
For one whose mind practices the breath, whose consciousness is devoted to the practice of air—
how?
In this manner, by this method.
What does not exist? Sleep.
Of what nature is it?
How is it appropriate?
What do we have?
Mere verbal recitation; the state of being a chatterbox.
Or how is it that "what" does not come to be?
It is the obstruction of air, the blocking of wind.
Why?
Because it does not occur suddenly through the force of violence.
Which recitation is not something to be studied through words?
What is it?
What is the nature of worship? It is the honoring of the deity; how is it characterized? It is appropriate.
What does not exist? Sacrificial rites such as the *homa* and so forth.
Of what nature is it?
It is to be abandoned;
how so?
In that manner, by that way;
in what? In meditative concentration (samādhi).
In this practice of accomplishing the swinging mantra. || 52 ||

Various acts of charity, numerous sacrifices, worship of deities, meditative concentration, moral conduct, resorting to all sacred fords, and the recitation of mantras—all these are not equal to this single practice of the breath-recitation (*prāṇajāpa*) which leads to imperishable auspiciousness; indeed, nothing else approaches it for the sake of sustaining the vital breath on all sides. (53)
"One should not go, one should not proceed"—
what does this mean?
It refers to the non-grasping that consists of the threefold gift.
What are the gift of material goods, the gift of fearlessness, and the gift of the Dharma? They are equal when weighed against one another.
Of what? Of this *prāṇajapa*. Of what nature is it?
Furthermore, of what kind of one?
Of one who has attained imperishable virtue, that is, one whose merit is indestructible.
Not only various gifts, but also worship and sacrifice— of what nature?
Very abundant, of many kinds.
Not only is there sacrifice, but also the worship of deities and the honoring of gods;
not only is there the worship of deities, but also meditative absorption and dhyāna;
and not only is there meditative absorption, but also moral conduct and the restraint of the five senses.
Not only is it moral conduct (*śīla*), but also resorting to sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and service to those sacred fords—
of what nature? Entire, that is, complete.

Not only should one not resort to sacred fords (*tīrtha*) or engage in the recitation of mantras (*mantra-jāpa*) and so forth, but why would one go to or perform various acts of giving (*dāna*) and the like? To what [end] would they be comparable? To what could they be equal?
For the sake of sustaining life and for the purpose of protecting life;
why? From all sides, everywhere.
How so? Because of which reason. || 53 ||

When the state [of the mind] is dissolved, the vital winds (marut) meet; thus, through the yoga of practice, one may effect nourishment, pacification, subjugation, as well as eradication and even slaying.
Whatever is desired shall be accomplished from the mere sight of these mandalas; furthermore, by obstructing them within their own bodies, supreme accomplishment (siddhi) itself shall arise. || 54 ||
Who should perform or performs it? The yogi.
What is that?
It is this; of what nature is it?
It is desired—that is, wished for.
Why?
Because of seeing— that is, because of beholding—
whom?
Why [are there] five mandalas among the mandalas? Because of the application of practice, that is, through effort.
Where is the mind?
When it meets— that is, becomes unified—
with what?
In what state of being are the Maruts, the winds?
In what state? Dissolved, completely melted away.
Of what nature was the desired object?
Nourishment and fullness—not merely nourishment; peace and tranquility—not merely tranquility; and mastery—meaning the state of being in control.
How so? Now,
it is not only subjugation (*vaśa*), eradication (*uccāṭana*), and expulsion (*udāsana*).
How?
Not in that manner, not by that way.
What would be the accomplishment— mundane or supramundane— that would result from merely performing expulsion and killing?
How? It is thus determined.
Why? Because of obstruction—that is, because of confinement—of what? Of these mandalas.
In what? In the body (vapuṣi), that is, the physical form.
From where? From beyond (parataḥ), meaning further on or afterwards. Of what nature? Supreme (uttamā), that is, great. || 54 || ,,,

Having understood this and thus abandoned attachment to all sense objects, the yogi—following the oral tradition of the guru—should quickly recite the mantra that is stainless and beyond verbal expression; having brought the vital breath under his own control, he should here fix the mind, which is like a shadow or an illusion, upon emptiness within the body. || 55 ||
Who maintains and composes it? The yogi. What?
The mind (manas) or consciousness (citta).
Where? Here, in emptiness—that is, in the samādhi of the emptiness of all phenomena.
Of what nature is the mind? Like a shadow, like an illusion, resembling a reflection or a magical apparition.
Having done what? Having brought it near, having established it.
Whom? The wind, the vital breath (prāṇavāyu).
Where? Here, in this body.
How? In this manner.
Having made it subject to oneself, that is, under one's own control; having recited what?
The mantra, namely the mantra of vajra-recitation.

Of what nature is it? It is devoid of vocal utterance, meaning it is free from the manifestation of speech. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is stainless, being free from all conceptual constructions.
How so? Swiftly, that is, quickly.
Why? From the tradition of the guru, that is, from the instruction of the guru.
Having done what? Having abandoned—having cast off—what? Attachment to all sense objects, namely, attachment to all objects such as form and the rest.
Having done what? Having known.
In what manner? In this way, by means of this method. || 55 ||

Or rather, having realized that earth, water, fire, wind, and so forth have false objects because they are devoid of being perceived as either one or many, one should contemplate this reality of emptiness—the essence of things—in order to bring stability to the mind; for when the mind is bound, the entire triple world is restrained and becomes itself [empty], like space.
