(56)
What comes to be? The mind, the consciousness; of what nature is it? That which is to be cultivated, that which is to be developed.
Of what nature is it? It is like space, resembling the sky.
What is to be done? To cause the sinful mind to attain what? Stability, that is, steadiness.
Having done what? Having known—that is, having awakened to—what? Earth, water, fire, air, and so forth. Of what nature are they? Having false objects—that is, having a deceptive essential nature.
How so? Or rather, how is it that the reality of the entity of emptiness (*śūnyatāvastutattva*) is like the reality of the substance of emptiness (*śūnyatādravyatattva*);
why? Because it is devoid of the apprehension of being one or many—that is, because it is free from the cognition of oneness or manifoldness.
What might it be? It would be the triple world, the three realms;
for what purpose, and of what nature? It is bound and withdrawn.
How? By oneself, by one's own self; how? For what reason? Under what condition? When the mind is bound, that is, when it is restrained. || 56 ||

Since, when analyzed through reasoning, the wind is seen to be like a flower in the sky, and since the entire threefold world arising therein appears like a dream, and since even the mind is unreal according to logic—what fruit could there be from false conceptualization? Therefore, this [reality] is certainly true and imperishable. (57)
What shines, what appears, and what expands? The mind; how is the mind characterized? It is the fruit.
Why? Because of false cultivation—that is, because of false latent impressions.
How so? What is meant by "how" and "what"? It is that which is non-existent.
By what reasoning, through the investigation of the scriptures, is there also the state of being without substance?
Of what nature is this mind? It is "being scrutinized" (carcyamāna), that is, being intensely examined;
what is it? The threefold existence (tribhava); like what? Like a dream (svapnavat), resembling a dream.
Of what nature is it? It is "akhilam," meaning entirely whole.
And of what nature is the mind? It is "khakusumasamam," meaning equal to a sky-flower. Of what nature is that [sky-flower]? It is "tatrodbhūtam," meaning arisen or produced therein.
Whom? Vāyu. By what? By what means (yukti). For what reason? From which cause.
Would it perish? Would it utterly vanish? Would it become false or unreal?
It is true; it is factual.
Of what nature is it? It is indestructible and imperishable.
How so? Certainly so.
Why? Because of inquiry.
Where? In this saṃsāra.
Of what nature is the truth? Constant, meaning immovable.
Why? For the reason that... || 57 ||
Since the mind is by nature auspicious, it is proper to meditate upon the true reality of the Self, which brings its own measure [of realization] and bestows supreme bliss.
However, that which is first meditated upon as being unreal must itself be made real; thus, O limb [of practice], one first washes away the impurity with extreme effort. || 58 ||
What occurs? The mind;
in what state? Joined, that is, properly engaged.
To do what? To meditate upon, to contemplate, to cultivate.
Of what nature [is it]? Naturally beautiful, pure by its very essence.
Why? Because:

Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is brought forth by its own means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that is, presented by its own measure. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*), the measure of the self.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is real (*tathya*), true (*satya*).
What is cultivated and contemplated? That mind.
Of what nature is it? It is real and authoritative. And how, having done what? Having meditated.
How? First, in the beginning, of what nature? "Atathā," meaning non-erroneous. How so? Because (yat), for which reason.
But how is it washed? What is it that is washed? That mind—having done what? Having done [it].
How? A limb, a part;
how? First;
of what nature? Impure, consisting of impurity.
Furthermore, of what nature was it? It was exceedingly painful and exceedingly miserable. || 58 ||

Nowhere at all does there exist another non-place such that every person clearly experiences it as a distinct portion of the directions belonging either to themselves or to another; for even such a portion, being formless, cannot exist without another portion, and thus it is not a single unity. Therefore, space (*dik*) does not exist in that way, because [the experience of direction] would otherwise be untenable.
Not only for oneself, but for another as well—
how so? Just as it is clearly seen that [the world] does not exist when analyzed.
What?
That which is without ground, without foundation;
of what nature? Beyond; where? Anywhere at all.
Of what? Of the directions, such as the east and so forth.
Of what nature? Being a part of a part, it is not non-existent.
What is it? A part (*bhāga*), which is also a portion (*aṃśa*).
Of what nature is it? Formless (*amūrta*) and non-existent in form (*asadrūpa*).
Why? Because of another division (*aparavibhāga*), that is, from something else.
How? For that reason;
how? In this manner; in what way? To the extent that...
What is it that does not exist? A single entity.
Why? Therefore:
Due to its removal— that is, because that other limb has ceased to exist— what direction is there?
Why? Because of non-connection, because of non-association.
How? In that manner, by that way. || 59 ||

That which has been accepted here by others as a real entity, such as the Self (ātman) and so forth—that cannot be established as one, because the other [concomitant] activities would be non-existent; therefore, it is not logical that the accomplishment of an effect occurs through a complete and unimpeded power via succession, for the claim that "an effect arises from a process of succession and not from non-succession" is false.
What is the nature of the categories—earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, and mind? They are real entities (sad-vastu) whose essential nature is substance (dravya-svarūpa).
Furthermore, what is their nature? They are accepted (svīkṛta) and emulated (anukṛta).
By whom? By others, such as the Vaiṣṇavas and so forth.
From what? Because of impermanence. Of what? Of actions, that is, of effects.
Of what kind? Of others, that is, different ones.
From where? Not from the sequence, that is, not in due order.
What? The accomplishment of the task. Of what nature? Appropriate.
Why? By way of sequence—that is, in due order.

Again, why? Because of the power of complete and unimpeded strength; because of the influence of a full, non-vacuous, and undestroyed radiance. What results from this? Its effect. Why? From sequential familiarity—that is, from knowledge of the proper order.
What does it not become? How is it unreal? Why? Because there is no sequential order. || 60 ||

If the eternal agent were to act immediately by his own will, then that will—whether falling into the two states of difference or non-difference—would either bring about the destruction of the agent or, if the mind were subject to a differentiated will, result in instability;
whereas from non-difference, the will would be constant. For one whose will is eternal, even a moment’s delay in action is not logical. (61)
In an instant, by what? By his own will, that is, by the will residing within himself. Of what nature is he? Eternal, meaning imperishable.
How? [The word] "vā" is used for inquiry; what would he perform or do? [The answer is] "icchā" (desire).
What [is the consequence]? The destruction of the agent, the destruction of the creator.
Being of what nature? Fallen into both difference and non-difference—that is, characterized by the duality of oneness and manifoldness—in whatever way possible.
It might be; who would it be? An agent.
Of what nature? One whose mind is under the control of another.
Why? Because of difference; it exists due to being distinct.
What is it? Firm desire.
Why? Because of non-difference, that is, because of oneness.
What does not exist? Delay.
Of what nature is it? Appropriate; that is, fitting.
Of whom? Of one who possesses eternal desire.
How? Even for a moment or even for a muhūrta.
In what? In what action or task. || 61 ||

If [the cause] acts as a co-producer through a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), then that entire complex is also produced by [other causes]; why, then, would this [complex] not produce its effect all at once?

If it is argued that this [complex] produces [the effect] only when supported [by a substratum], that too is unproven, for [such a substratum] is impossible due to [the cause's] lack of connection, and because it would contradict the nature of the class of entities (*arthajāti*) which possesses parts. || 62 ||
Who performed [it]? The agent.
Of what nature was he? One who acts with assistance, one who acts in conjunction.
By what? By the totality, by the collection.
How? If that [collection] also...
What is this? It is this causal complex (*sāmagrī*), which is a collection. Of what nature is it? It is "entire" (*sarvā*), meaning complete.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "produced by that," meaning created by God (*īśvara*).
Who does not act? Who does not do [it]? Is this the agent? What is the action?
How? All at once, that is, in a single moment.
How so? Why does it not produce, why does it not bring forth? Who? This agent.
What is the causal complex?
How?
And if one asks what its nature is, it is the substratum.
He who possesses a bowl for carrying [alms] exists. Who is he?
This is the agent.
Of what nature is he?
Unestablished, that is, unproduced.
Why?
Because of non-association, that is, because of non-contact. How so?

The agent. Of what nature? Possessing a body with parts; that is, having a physical form composed of constituent parts.
When what exists?
In conjunction.
Why?
Because of contradiction. Of what? Of a class of objects, that is, a class of phenomena (*dharmajāti*). How so? || 62 ||
Therefore, one should behold the world—which is empty, innate, stainless, signless, luminous, and like the sky.
What? Saṃsāra.
That is the pacification of those [afflictions] or liberation;
it is not merely the pacification of those, nor the self alone,
nor merely the self, nor another such as an agent and so forth.
How so?
Now, it is not only the other [factors] such as the seer and the seen.
How?
In that manner, by that way. || 63-64 ||

There is no means whatsoever for anyone to enter into that space which is free from modification, because it is all-pervasive in every respect; likewise, there is no possibility of any means anywhere for that which is all-encompassing, immovable, fire-like, and entirely devoid of danger—that which is called emptiness (śūnyatā).
It does not exist at all.
What?
A means.
Someone asks:
for what purpose?
For the sake of entering together.
In what?
In some space.
Of what nature?
"Free from modification" means devoid of transformation.
Why?
Because of its all-pervasiveness.
Why? From everywhere; that is, in every place.
How?
For example:
how?
Exceedingly.
There is none. What?
Origination, that is, arising.
Where?
Nowhere at all;
in that which is called emptiness, namely, in emptiness itself.
How?
In that manner, by that way.
Of what?
Of the means (upāya). Of what nature is that which is called emptiness (śūnyatā)?
Pervading the universe, consisting of the world.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
One whose mind is unwavering, that is, one whose intellect is steady.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
In that which is devoid of misfortune and free from the suffering of all conceptual constructions;
why? Because it is everywhere and in every respect. || 65 ||

Just as some ignorant person, having constructed a ladder here on earth, enters into the sky through delusion, emerges from it, and takes pleasure there—even while taking hold of deities and the like—so too, having prepared [the mind] in such a way, one becomes absorbed in knowledge through error; thus he remains and rejoices in himself. (66)
"He enters" means he makes an entrance.
Who? The ignorant one.
Who?
Someone here in the empty space. By what?
"By delusion" means through error.
Having done what?
Having performed [it].
What? Ascending, mounting, or going upwards. By what?
By means of a ladder, that is, by way of a flight of steps;
where?
Here, in this cycle of existence.
How?
Just as he emerges and is gladdened, he becomes joyful.
How?
Likewise;
it happens.
Who?
This one is ignorant and deluded. Of what nature?
Submerged and sunk.
In what?
In knowledge. How is that?
Having done what? Having prepared, that is, having made.
What?
Taking the gods and so forth as an object means relying upon the gods and so forth. In what way?
How?
Thus he rejoices, plays,
and remains.
How?
One's own [nature] by oneself. || 66 ||

Just as a person whose mind is deluded might desire the pervasion of the sky or water while remaining right there, following after it, possessing its nature, and longing for it; even so, one whose intellect is struck by error might pray for the attainment of knowledge, disregarding one's own true nature which is of the form of consciousness, beginningless, and unborn. // 67 //
One should desire; one should long for.
Who?
A person of dull intellect, a person of weak understanding.
What?
The pervasion of space, the extension of the ether. Like what?
Just as;
how is he?
He is one who has no state.
Where?
There, in the water (or jar).
Furthermore, what is its further qualification?
Following that, he is one who conforms to the cognition of water therein;
furthermore, what is his qualification? He is of that nature, having that as his essence.
Furthermore, what is his specific characteristic? He desires that; he strives for it; he prays for it, he entreats it.
Who?
The person whose mind is struck by delusion, whose intellect is destroyed by ignorance.
What?
The attainment of knowledge, the attainment of reality.
Like what?
In that same way, exactly so. How so? Doing what? Disregarding, that is, not knowing.
What? One's own self.
Of what nature?
It has the form of knowledge and is the very nature of knowledge. Furthermore, how is it qualified?
It is of a nature that is primordially unarisen, having as its essential character the non-arising from the very beginning. || 67 ||
"I am the cultivator of this reality from which darkness has been dispelled; through this meditative absorption, may great accomplishment in the *mudrā* arise for me instantly.
Where is even the mention of such a person whose mind is fixed on duality? It is like one who, through delusion, seeks to smell the fragrance of a flower born of the sky.
There is no one.
